task.goal: Find a practical way to reduce false freezer-temperature alarms in a food bank while still catching genuine warming events.
hard_constraints: One technician has four days and can inspect two existing sensors and archived minute-level temperatures; no new hardware purchase.
Food may not be deliberately warmed and alarm coverage may not be disabled during staffed or unstaffed hours.
Distinguish sensor placement, door-opening transients and sensor drift; include a check that a proposed change does not mask a true sustained excursion.
task.available_resources: Two spare calibrated thermometers and staff door-opening notes.
task.expected_result: A reversible diagnosis and mitigation with a small validation plan.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Correct an unrepresentative sensor location
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: move an alarm sensor away from a local airflow or doorway artifact to a location that better represents stored-food conditions. A short air-temperature spike near the door can trigger alarms even when the storage zone remains cold. This approach changes the measurement location rather than the alarm threshold.

During days 1–2, keep both existing sensors and all alarms operating. Compare each sensor with a spare calibrated thermometer placed beside it, allowing equilibration. Then use the spare thermometers to compare the current positions with plausible storage-zone positions during normal operation. Match temperature traces to staff door-opening notes. Close agreement between colocated instruments but different temperatures across locations suggests placement; simultaneous short peaks tied to door notes suggest door transients; persistent disagreement between colocated instruments suggests sensor bias or drift. A single comparison establishes bias, not historical drift.

If placement is implicated, relocate only one sensor at a time on day 3, leaving the second active and ensuring continuous alarm coverage during the move. Preserve settings and record the original position for reversal. Observe through day 4. This requires movable sensors, suitable thermometer resolution and a location consistent with existing food-safety requirements. Avoid choosing the coldest location merely because it produces fewer alarms. If continuous coverage or representative placement cannot be established, leave the installation unchanged.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the relocated sensor with its original-position record under similar ordinary door activity, using the unchanged sensor and thermometer checks as references. Falsify the proposal if alarms decline only because the new position consistently reads colder than representative storage locations. Inspect archived sustained warming events, if available, and confirm the proposed position responds promptly to naturally occurring broader warming observed during the trial. An offline sustained-rise replay can check alarm logic but cannot establish the thermal responsiveness of an untested location. Without adequate physical evidence, retain the original placement and report the diagnosis as provisional; do not deliberately warm food.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use bounded persistence for short door-opening spikes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distinguish a brief threshold crossing from sustained warming using a bounded persistence rule, while retaining immediate protection at a higher temperature. This can reduce nuisance notifications without moving sensors or treating door notes as permission to suppress alarms.

On day 1, inspect both sensor positions and compare each sensor with a colocated calibrated thermometer. Repeat comparisons after equilibration and on subsequent days to identify persistent bias or changing disagreement. Analyze archived minute-level readings alongside staff door notes to separate likely door transients from sustained or unexplained events. Correct or flag measurement problems before selecting timing parameters.

Prototype a rule that issues the usual actionable alarm when the normal threshold remains exceeded for a short, explicitly limited duration, and issues an immediate alarm at the existing critical limit. Never restart the persistence timer merely because another door opening is noted. Keep fault, missing-data and critical-temperature alarms immediate. Choose the maximum delay from established food-safety limits and response requirements, not just from how long nuisance spikes last.

Days 2–3 are for offline replay; day 4 is for shadow operation alongside unchanged live alarms. Implementation requires configurable alarm software or an existing processing interface, timestamps and documented allowable response delays. Enable the rule only if those prerequisites and validation support it; otherwise deliver the reversible configuration for further review. Alarm coverage remains active throughout. Two sensors should not be required to agree before detecting warming, because localized warming or a failed sensor could otherwise be missed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare proposed notifications with the current instantaneous-threshold rule on held-out archive periods. Count removed short events and measure detection delay for every known sustained excursion. Add explicitly synthetic offline traces containing slow ramps, abrupt sustained rises, repeated door-like peaks on a rising baseline, and one failed or missing sensor. Reject the rule if any sustained excursion is missed or detection exceeds the predefined allowable delay. If archives lack genuine excursions, state that synthetic replay validates software behavior only; shadow operation alone does not prove safety.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reduce the door events that generate nuisance alarms
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce warm-air entry through changes to routine freezer access, keeping sensor positions and alarm rules intact. Preparing pick lists outside the freezer, staging carts before opening, assigning one person to coordinate retrieval and checking that the door fully closes may reduce both false alarms and actual temperature disturbance. This is most useful when alarms follow avoidable prolonged or closely repeated openings.

On day 1, inspect the two sensor locations and compare each sensor against a colocated spare calibrated thermometer. Repeat checks after equilibration and later in the trial. Agreement locally but different doorway versus storage-zone behavior indicates a placement effect; brief peaks synchronized with door notes support door transients; persistent or changing disagreement with a reference suggests bias or possible drift. Do not interpret fewer alarms as proof that sensor drift has disappeared.

Use archived readings and notes on day 2 to identify the access patterns most associated with alarms. Agree with staff on one simple workflow change, then trial it during ordinary work on days 3–4. Keep necessary access unrestricted, avoid consolidating work into a single excessively long opening, and keep every existing alarm active during staffed and unstaffed hours. Record opening duration, approximate workload and alarm times. The technician needs staff cooperation, existing notes and ordinary observation; no new hardware or alarm integration is needed.

This is immediately reversible and preserves existing sustained-excursion detection. Its limits are staff adherence, incomplete door records and causes unrelated to access, such as refrigeration faults, poor placement or sensor drift. It may produce little benefit if door openings are already brief and well managed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare trial periods with archived periods having similar workload and opening counts, using the unchanged alarm system as the comparator. Look for shorter cumulative door-open time and fewer brief peaks without an increase in baseline temperature, maximum temperature or recovery time. Reject the workflow if it merely shifts access into longer openings or does not reduce nuisance events. Confirm unchanged alarm settings and replay a recorded sustained excursion, or an explicitly synthetic sustained rise, through the existing logic offline. This checks continued alarm behavior without warming food; a four-day observation cannot establish long-term effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Correct a verified sensor calibration bias
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: remove a confirmed positive measurement bias using an existing, manufacturer-supported calibration adjustment. A sensor that consistently reads too warm can generate false alarms even at a representative location. Correcting its measurement can reduce those alarms while preserving the temperature limits and immediate alarm behavior. This differs from relocating a sensor or delaying notifications.

On days 1–2, keep both sensors and all alarms operating. Place one spare calibrated thermometer beside each sensor without touching walls or obstructing airflow, allow equilibration, and record paired readings during stable periods and normal door activity. Swap the reference thermometers between positions to check whether disagreement follows the installed sensor or a reference instrument. Inspect mounting and archived readings alongside door-opening notes. Local agreement with different temperatures between positions supports placement effects; brief locally corroborated peaks associated with openings support door transients; repeatable disagreement at the same position supports calibration bias. Changing disagreement suggests possible drift, but four days cannot establish its long-term rate.

Proceed only if one sensor has a stable positive bias exceeding reference uncertainty, the adjustment is supported, and observed conditions adequately cover the temperatures where correction matters. Do not compensate an unstable or temperature-dependent error with a single offset. On day 3, save the original configuration and apply the verified correction to that sensor while maintaining continuous alarm coverage; observe through day 4. Restore the original configuration if checks fail.

This requires access to existing calibration settings and assurance that configuration changes preserve coverage. If those prerequisites are absent, or comparison data are inadequate, retain the existing settings and report the fault. No hardware purchase or deliberate warming is needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare corrected readings with the independent reference and the original readings during ordinary operation. Reject the adjustment if it causes under-reading beyond the documented measurement tolerance, fails after swapping references, or varies materially with temperature. Replay archived sustained excursions where independent evidence supports their interpretation. Also test explicitly synthetic true-temperature ramps and sustained steps with plausible sensor errors through the corrected alarm logic, comparing detection against an unbiased sensor using the unchanged thresholds. Reject any correction that misses a sustained excursion or exceeds the established response requirement. Synthetic replay checks logic, not calibration outside the observed range; absent adequate temperature-range evidence, leave the correction unapplied.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair an intermittent sensor connection that creates spurious warm readings
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: eliminate an intermittent measurement fault at an existing sensor connector or cable termination. A loose connection or moisture at a connector can produce erroneous readings in some sensor systems; whether it can resemble warming depends on the sensor and controller. Repairing a verified connection fault changes measurement reliability without changing placement, calibration offsets or alarm timing.

On day 1, inspect both sensor installations, accessible cables and controller diagnostics. Keep both alarms active. Place a calibrated thermometer beside each sensor, allow equilibration, and compare readings during stable conditions and ordinary door openings. Use archived minute-level temperatures and staff notes to identify abrupt jumps, dropouts or implausible recovery patterns, but do not classify events as false from their shape alone.

On day 2, swap the reference thermometers and repeat comparisons. Locally corroborated brief rises associated with openings support door transients; agreement locally but different behavior between locations supports placement effects; persistent or progressively changing disagreement supports bias or possible drift. Abrupt disagreement accompanied by connection-related diagnostics or visible connector damage supports an intermittent signal fault. Four days cannot establish long-term drift.

If evidence identifies a serviceable connection fault, perform only manufacturer-supported cleaning, drying, reseating or tightening on day 3, using existing supplies. Record the original arrangement and observe through day 4. This requires technician competence, accessible service documentation and a repair that preserves continuous alarm coverage. If servicing interrupts a channel, proceed only where the other active channel independently provides adequate coverage throughout; otherwise leave the connection untouched. Do not replace parts, bypass faults or suppress notifications. The approach offers no benefit when both independent instruments confirm actual warming.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare disagreement with the calibrated references and the frequency of unexplained jumps before and after repair, retaining unchanged alarm settings as the comparator. Reject the diagnosis if warm peaks remain independently corroborated or disagreement persists. Verify that servicing has not introduced under-reading or slower response during ordinary temperature changes. Replay an archived sustained excursion, if available, and an explicitly synthetic sustained rise through the unchanged alarm logic to check continued detection. Replay cannot establish physical sensor responsiveness; if reference comparisons or naturally occurring changes leave that uncertain, report the repair as provisionally validated and retain all alarms.

EXPAND.title: Correct a verified sensor calibration error
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: correct a demonstrated warm-reading measurement bias so that normal freezer temperatures no longer cross the alarm threshold incorrectly. This changes measurement accuracy rather than sensor placement or alarm timing. It is useful only if one of the existing sensors measurably disagrees with calibrated references.

On day 1, inspect both installations and place one spare calibrated thermometer beside each sensor without moving the sensors or interrupting alarms. Allow equilibration and record paired readings during stable conditions and ordinary door openings. On day 2, exchange the reference thermometers and repeat. Disagreement that follows an existing sensor supports sensor bias; disagreement that follows a reference calls the comparison into question. Agreement between colocated instruments, combined with differences between locations, supports placement effects. Brief rises shared by colocated instruments and aligned with door notes support actual door transients. Changing sensor-reference disagreement suggests instability; historical drift cannot be established from a single offset check.

If a stable bias exceeds combined measurement uncertainty, use the manufacturer's supported calibration procedure on day 3, provided continuous alarm coverage can be maintained. Preserve the original configuration and verify the corrected readings independently through day 4. Do not apply a blanket offset to a sensor whose error varies with temperature or time.

Prerequisites are accessible readings, suitable reference accuracy at freezer temperatures, supported calibration controls and an established acceptable error. No purchase is needed. If calibration requires interrupting required coverage, or the references cannot establish a reliable correction, leave the configuration unchanged and document the fault. The change is reversible, although restoring a known inaccurate setting would require appropriate operational judgment.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare corrected and original readings against the independent references, using unchanged measurements as the comparator. Reject the correction if it improves agreement only at one condition, creates cold-reading bias, or fails the reference-swap check. Replay archived sustained excursions and explicitly synthetic sustained rises offline with the proposed correction applied. Confirm alarm detection stays within established response requirements, including when only the corrected sensor warms. Replay checks logic; actual calibration accuracy requires physical reference agreement. Four days cannot establish long-term stability.

EXPAND.title: Restore proper door sealing using existing components
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: eliminate unintended warm-air leakage caused by a preventable closure defect. A package obstructing the door, debris on the sealing surface or a displaced serviceable gasket can extend temperature disturbances after staff believe the door is closed. Removing the physical cause can reduce alarms while leaving their detection rules intact. These alarms may reflect real local warming rather than inaccurate measurements.

On day 1, inspect both sensor locations and compare each with a colocated calibrated thermometer. Repeat after equilibration and later in the trial. Local instrument agreement with different behavior across locations suggests placement; short shared rises aligned with door notes suggest opening transients; persistent or changing disagreement against references suggests bias or possible drift. Use archived traces and notes to identify episodes with unusually slow recovery after reported closure.

On day 2, inspect the door perimeter, closure path and existing gasket during normal access. Check for trapped packaging, frost or debris and visibly displaced components. Correct only simple defects within the technician's competence and the equipment's maintenance instructions, such as removing an obstruction or cleaning an approved sealing surface. Do not assume a defective gasket can be repaired without replacement parts. Avoid prolonged inspection openings, and keep all alarms operating throughout.

Observe normal operation on days 3–4, recording closure observations, access activity and temperature recovery. Preserve photographs or notes of the original condition and any reversible adjustment. This requires an identifiable closure defect and maintenance that can safely occur without interrupting alarm coverage. If the door already seals correctly, this mechanism offers no expected benefit. Refrigeration faults, sensor errors and normal opening transients remain separate possibilities.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare post-maintenance recovery and closed-door temperature behavior with archived periods having similar access and starting temperatures. The comparator is the original door condition with identical alarm settings. Reject the diagnosis if closure improves visibly but slow recovery and nuisance alarms persist, or if baseline temperature rises. Verify both sensors remain active with unchanged thresholds, and replay an archived or explicitly synthetic sustained excursion through the unchanged alarm logic offline. This confirms continued logical detection without warming food; it does not prove refrigeration performance under an actual fault.

EXPAND.title: Repair a demonstrated temperature-data interpretation fault
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: remove false alarms introduced between measurement and notification, such as stale readings presented as current, incorrect unit conversion or a channel mapped to the wrong freezer. This changes data interpretation rather than the physical temperature, placement or alarm persistence. It is independently useful only if the available system exposes enough information to demonstrate such a fault.

On day 1, inspect the two sensors and compare their local readings with colocated calibrated thermometers. Repeat stable comparisons to distinguish persistent bias from possible changing error. Compare locations and match ordinary temperature peaks to staff door notes to separate placement effects and opening transients. Reference checks establish physical measurement behavior before blaming the software.

On day 2, trace several archived alarm episodes from sensor identity and timestamp through the displayed value and notification. Check units, channel names, timestamp conventions and whether recorded values represent fresh samples. A missing link is uncertainty, not proof of a software fault. Restrict investigation to accessible records and existing configuration; do not assume source-code access or invent a failed component.

If a specific error is demonstrated, prepare the smallest reversible configuration correction and replay it offline on day 3. On day 4, compare its outputs with unchanged live alarms in shadow operation. A live correction is appropriate only if supported controls allow continuous coverage and validation succeeds; otherwise deliver the diagnosed fault and tested configuration for later application. Preserve existing sensor-fault and missing-data alarms. A stale warm reading must become an explicit data-quality fault rather than silently disappearing.

The technician needs accessible logs or displays and documented field meanings. Some installations will lack these capabilities, making this a diagnosis-only option within four days.
EXPAND.experiment: For a small set of disputed alarms, compare the interpreted value with the contemporaneous source reading and independent reference where available. Reject the proposal if no reproducible interpretation error exists. Replay known sustained excursions and explicitly synthetic sustained rises separately on each channel, plus stale and missing samples. Require correct channel identification, timely warming alarms and explicit fault reporting. The comparator is the current interpretation of identical input records. Any genuine excursion lost through remapping, conversion or freshness handling falsifies the proposed correction; synthetic replay establishes software behavior only.

EXPAND.title: Prevent repeated alarms from one unresolved temperature episode
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use hysteresis when rearming temperature alarms. After the first threshold crossing triggers an immediate alarm, keep that episode open until temperature falls below a separate, lower recovery threshold. Small oscillations around the alarm threshold then remain one episode instead of generating repeated new alarms. This can reduce nuisance alarms where repeated threshold crossings dominate; it does not eliminate the first alarm caused by a door opening.

On day 1, inspect both sensors and compare each with a colocated spare calibrated thermometer after equilibration. Exchange the references and repeat on day 2. Agreement locally but differences between locations support placement effects; shared brief rises associated with door notes support door-opening transients; persistent sensor-reference disagreement supports bias. Changing disagreement suggests possible drift, but four days cannot establish long-term drift reliably.

Use archived minute-level temperatures and available alarm records to determine whether repeated notifications actually arise from rearming near the threshold. If they do, prepare a reversible recovery-threshold setting using existing supported controls. Keep the initial alarm threshold unchanged. Keep the episode visibly active, preserve required reminders and escalation, and retain immediate critical-temperature and sensor-fault notifications. Each sensor must independently trigger protection. Acknowledgement must not count as temperature recovery.

The technician can inspect and diagnose on days 1–2, replay the proposed setting on day 3 and observe it in shadow operation on day 4. Live implementation requires documented alarm-state behavior and controls that preserve continuous coverage; otherwise leave live settings unchanged and deliver the configuration for review. Save the original settings. This approach offers little benefit if alarms are isolated events or operational policy requires every repeated crossing to generate a new notification.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare existing behavior with the proposed rearming rule on the same archived traces. Count redundant episode starts, while checking that every initial threshold crossing still alarms at the same minute. Inspect any archived sustained excursions. If none exist, also replay explicitly synthetic sustained rises, including a rise beginning while an episode is already active: it must retain active warning, required reminders and critical escalation. Reject the change if it clears an unresolved event, delays initial detection or suppresses escalation. Synthetic replay checks logic only; four days of shadow observation cannot establish long-term safety or effectiveness.

REFINE.title: Repair candidate 2: stage retrievals outside without lengthening openings
REFINE.proposal: Original candidate index: 2. Its strongest practical advantage is reducing door-related disturbances while preserving existing alarm protection. Exact weakness: its suggested coordination and consolidation can turn several short retrievals into one prolonged opening, increasing warming even if alarm counts fall. Changed action: trial only outside-the-freezer preparation—finish the pick list and stage the cart before opening, retrieve one ordinary load, and fully close the door before sorting or preparing another trip. Do not batch additional loads into a longer opening. This makes the intervention specific and reversible while directly reducing avoidable open-door time. On days 1–2, keep all alarms active, compare both sensors with colocated calibrated thermometers after equilibration, swap references, and match archived temperatures to door notes. Local agreement with spatial differences supports placement effects; corroborated brief peaks linked to openings support door transients; persistent disagreement supports bias, while changing disagreement suggests possible drift. Trial the preparation change on days 3–4 only if door transients are implicated. Prerequisites are staff cooperation and a usable staging area outside the freezer. Remaining limit: four days and incomplete door notes cannot establish long-term effectiveness or exclude refrigeration faults.
REFINE.experiment: Record opening durations, retrieval workload and temperature recovery during the trial; compare with ordinary retrievals of similar workload from days 1–2 and suitable archived periods. Falsify the repair if preparation leads to longer openings, higher between-opening temperatures or slower recovery, even if alarm counts decrease. Preserve sensor positions, thresholds and notification paths throughout staffed and unstaffed hours. Replay one recorded sustained excursion, or an explicitly synthetic sustained rise if none exists, through the unchanged alarm logic to confirm it still triggers at the existing threshold and timing. This checks logic without warming food; it does not establish physical sensor responsiveness. Revert the workflow if the thermal checks fail.

SAVE.title: Correct an unrepresentative sensor location
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: move an alarm sensor away from a local airflow or doorway artifact to a location that better represents stored-food conditions. A short air-temperature spike near the door can trigger alarms even when the storage zone remains cold. This approach changes the measurement location rather than the alarm threshold.

During days 1–2, keep both existing sensors and all alarms operating. Compare each sensor with a spare calibrated thermometer placed beside it, allowing equilibration. Then use the spare thermometers to compare the current positions with plausible storage-zone positions during normal operation. Match temperature traces to staff door-opening notes. Close agreement between colocated instruments but different temperatures across locations suggests placement; simultaneous short peaks tied to door notes suggest door transients; persistent disagreement between colocated instruments suggests sensor bias or drift. A single comparison establishes bias, not historical drift.

If placement is implicated, relocate only one sensor at a time on day 3, leaving the second active and ensuring continuous alarm coverage during the move. Preserve settings and record the original position for reversal. Observe through day 4. This requires movable sensors, suitable thermometer resolution and a location consistent with existing food-safety requirements. Avoid choosing the coldest location merely because it produces fewer alarms. If continuous coverage or representative placement cannot be established, leave the installation unchanged.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the relocated sensor with its original-position record under similar ordinary door activity, using the unchanged sensor and thermometer checks as references. Falsify the proposal if alarms decline only because the new position consistently reads colder than representative storage locations. Inspect archived sustained warming events, if available, and confirm the proposed position responds promptly to naturally occurring broader warming observed during the trial. An offline sustained-rise replay can check alarm logic but cannot establish the thermal responsiveness of an untested location. Without adequate physical evidence, retain the original placement and report the diagnosis as provisional; do not deliberately warm food.

SAVE.title: Use bounded persistence for short door-opening spikes
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: distinguish a brief threshold crossing from sustained warming using a bounded persistence rule, while retaining immediate protection at a higher temperature. This can reduce nuisance notifications without moving sensors or treating door notes as permission to suppress alarms.

On day 1, inspect both sensor positions and compare each sensor with a colocated calibrated thermometer. Repeat comparisons after equilibration and on subsequent days to identify persistent bias or changing disagreement. Analyze archived minute-level readings alongside staff door notes to separate likely door transients from sustained or unexplained events. Correct or flag measurement problems before selecting timing parameters.

Prototype a rule that issues the usual actionable alarm when the normal threshold remains exceeded for a short, explicitly limited duration, and issues an immediate alarm at the existing critical limit. Never restart the persistence timer merely because another door opening is noted. Keep fault, missing-data and critical-temperature alarms immediate. Choose the maximum delay from established food-safety limits and response requirements, not just from how long nuisance spikes last.

Days 2–3 are for offline replay; day 4 is for shadow operation alongside unchanged live alarms. Implementation requires configurable alarm software or an existing processing interface, timestamps and documented allowable response delays. Enable the rule only if those prerequisites and validation support it; otherwise deliver the reversible configuration for further review. Alarm coverage remains active throughout. Two sensors should not be required to agree before detecting warming, because localized warming or a failed sensor could otherwise be missed.
SAVE.experiment: Compare proposed notifications with the current instantaneous-threshold rule on held-out archive periods. Count removed short events and measure detection delay for every known sustained excursion. Add explicitly synthetic offline traces containing slow ramps, abrupt sustained rises, repeated door-like peaks on a rising baseline, and one failed or missing sensor. Reject the rule if any sustained excursion is missed or detection exceeds the predefined allowable delay. If archives lack genuine excursions, state that synthetic replay validates software behavior only; shadow operation alone does not prove safety.

SAVE.title: Reduce the door events that generate nuisance alarms
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce warm-air entry through changes to routine freezer access, keeping sensor positions and alarm rules intact. Preparing pick lists outside the freezer, staging carts before opening, assigning one person to coordinate retrieval and checking that the door fully closes may reduce both false alarms and actual temperature disturbance. This is most useful when alarms follow avoidable prolonged or closely repeated openings.

On day 1, inspect the two sensor locations and compare each sensor against a colocated spare calibrated thermometer. Repeat checks after equilibration and later in the trial. Agreement locally but different doorway versus storage-zone behavior indicates a placement effect; brief peaks synchronized with door notes support door transients; persistent or changing disagreement with a reference suggests bias or possible drift. Do not interpret fewer alarms as proof that sensor drift has disappeared.

Use archived readings and notes on day 2 to identify the access patterns most associated with alarms. Agree with staff on one simple workflow change, then trial it during ordinary work on days 3–4. Keep necessary access unrestricted, avoid consolidating work into a single excessively long opening, and keep every existing alarm active during staffed and unstaffed hours. Record opening duration, approximate workload and alarm times. The technician needs staff cooperation, existing notes and ordinary observation; no new hardware or alarm integration is needed.

This is immediately reversible and preserves existing sustained-excursion detection. Its limits are staff adherence, incomplete door records and causes unrelated to access, such as refrigeration faults, poor placement or sensor drift. It may produce little benefit if door openings are already brief and well managed.
SAVE.experiment: Compare trial periods with archived periods having similar workload and opening counts, using the unchanged alarm system as the comparator. Look for shorter cumulative door-open time and fewer brief peaks without an increase in baseline temperature, maximum temperature or recovery time. Reject the workflow if it merely shifts access into longer openings or does not reduce nuisance events. Confirm unchanged alarm settings and replay a recorded sustained excursion, or an explicitly synthetic sustained rise, through the existing logic offline. This checks continued alarm behavior without warming food; a four-day observation cannot establish long-term effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Correct a verified sensor calibration error
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: correct a demonstrated warm-reading measurement bias so that normal freezer temperatures no longer cross the alarm threshold incorrectly. This changes measurement accuracy rather than sensor placement or alarm timing. It is useful only if one of the existing sensors measurably disagrees with calibrated references.

On day 1, inspect both installations and place one spare calibrated thermometer beside each sensor without moving the sensors or interrupting alarms. Allow equilibration and record paired readings during stable conditions and ordinary door openings. On day 2, exchange the reference thermometers and repeat. Disagreement that follows an existing sensor supports sensor bias; disagreement that follows a reference calls the comparison into question. Agreement between colocated instruments, combined with differences between locations, supports placement effects. Brief rises shared by colocated instruments and aligned with door notes support actual door transients. Changing sensor-reference disagreement suggests instability; historical drift cannot be established from a single offset check.

If a stable bias exceeds combined measurement uncertainty, use the manufacturer's supported calibration procedure on day 3, provided continuous alarm coverage can be maintained. Preserve the original configuration and verify the corrected readings independently through day 4. Do not apply a blanket offset to a sensor whose error varies with temperature or time.

Prerequisites are accessible readings, suitable reference accuracy at freezer temperatures, supported calibration controls and an established acceptable error. No purchase is needed. If calibration requires interrupting required coverage, or the references cannot establish a reliable correction, leave the configuration unchanged and document the fault. The change is reversible, although restoring a known inaccurate setting would require appropriate operational judgment.
SAVE.experiment: Compare corrected and original readings against the independent references, using unchanged measurements as the comparator. Reject the correction if it improves agreement only at one condition, creates cold-reading bias, or fails the reference-swap check. Replay archived sustained excursions and explicitly synthetic sustained rises offline with the proposed correction applied. Confirm alarm detection stays within established response requirements, including when only the corrected sensor warms. Replay checks logic; actual calibration accuracy requires physical reference agreement. Four days cannot establish long-term stability.

SAVE.title: Restore proper door sealing using existing components
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: eliminate unintended warm-air leakage caused by a preventable closure defect. A package obstructing the door, debris on the sealing surface or a displaced serviceable gasket can extend temperature disturbances after staff believe the door is closed. Removing the physical cause can reduce alarms while leaving their detection rules intact. These alarms may reflect real local warming rather than inaccurate measurements.

On day 1, inspect both sensor locations and compare each with a colocated calibrated thermometer. Repeat after equilibration and later in the trial. Local instrument agreement with different behavior across locations suggests placement; short shared rises aligned with door notes suggest opening transients; persistent or changing disagreement against references suggests bias or possible drift. Use archived traces and notes to identify episodes with unusually slow recovery after reported closure.

On day 2, inspect the door perimeter, closure path and existing gasket during normal access. Check for trapped packaging, frost or debris and visibly displaced components. Correct only simple defects within the technician's competence and the equipment's maintenance instructions, such as removing an obstruction or cleaning an approved sealing surface. Do not assume a defective gasket can be repaired without replacement parts. Avoid prolonged inspection openings, and keep all alarms operating throughout.

Observe normal operation on days 3–4, recording closure observations, access activity and temperature recovery. Preserve photographs or notes of the original condition and any reversible adjustment. This requires an identifiable closure defect and maintenance that can safely occur without interrupting alarm coverage. If the door already seals correctly, this mechanism offers no expected benefit. Refrigeration faults, sensor errors and normal opening transients remain separate possibilities.
SAVE.experiment: Compare post-maintenance recovery and closed-door temperature behavior with archived periods having similar access and starting temperatures. The comparator is the original door condition with identical alarm settings. Reject the diagnosis if closure improves visibly but slow recovery and nuisance alarms persist, or if baseline temperature rises. Verify both sensors remain active with unchanged thresholds, and replay an archived or explicitly synthetic sustained excursion through the unchanged alarm logic offline. This confirms continued logical detection without warming food; it does not prove refrigeration performance under an actual fault.

SAVE.title: Repair a demonstrated temperature-data interpretation fault
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: remove false alarms introduced between measurement and notification, such as stale readings presented as current, incorrect unit conversion or a channel mapped to the wrong freezer. This changes data interpretation rather than the physical temperature, placement or alarm persistence. It is independently useful only if the available system exposes enough information to demonstrate such a fault.

On day 1, inspect the two sensors and compare their local readings with colocated calibrated thermometers. Repeat stable comparisons to distinguish persistent bias from possible changing error. Compare locations and match ordinary temperature peaks to staff door notes to separate placement effects and opening transients. Reference checks establish physical measurement behavior before blaming the software.

On day 2, trace several archived alarm episodes from sensor identity and timestamp through the displayed value and notification. Check units, channel names, timestamp conventions and whether recorded values represent fresh samples. A missing link is uncertainty, not proof of a software fault. Restrict investigation to accessible records and existing configuration; do not assume source-code access or invent a failed component.

If a specific error is demonstrated, prepare the smallest reversible configuration correction and replay it offline on day 3. On day 4, compare its outputs with unchanged live alarms in shadow operation. A live correction is appropriate only if supported controls allow continuous coverage and validation succeeds; otherwise deliver the diagnosed fault and tested configuration for later application. Preserve existing sensor-fault and missing-data alarms. A stale warm reading must become an explicit data-quality fault rather than silently disappearing.

The technician needs accessible logs or displays and documented field meanings. Some installations will lack these capabilities, making this a diagnosis-only option within four days.
SAVE.experiment: For a small set of disputed alarms, compare the interpreted value with the contemporaneous source reading and independent reference where available. Reject the proposal if no reproducible interpretation error exists. Replay known sustained excursions and explicitly synthetic sustained rises separately on each channel, plus stale and missing samples. Require correct channel identification, timely warming alarms and explicit fault reporting. The comparator is the current interpretation of identical input records. Any genuine excursion lost through remapping, conversion or freshness handling falsifies the proposed correction; synthetic replay establishes software behavior only.
